title: Mira Nair's 'Amri' Is the Diaspora Art Film We've Been Waiting For
excerpt: A Hungarian-Indian painter, a diaspora filmmaker, and Priyanka Chopra walk into a biopic — and for once, the result might actually honour the original.
body:
Mira Nair has spent four decades making films about people who exist between worlds — the street kids of Bombay, the Ugandan-Indian shopkeepers of 'Mississippi Masala,' the marriage-obsessed family of 'Monsoon Wedding.' Now, with 'Amri,' she's found perhaps her most personal subject yet: Amrita Sher-Gil, the Hungarian-Indian modernist painter who died at 28 and left behind a body of work that fundamentally changed how India sees itself through art.

## The Artist Who Saw India First

For those unfamiliar with Amrita Sher-Gil, a primer: born in 1913 in Budapest to a Sikh father and Hungarian mother, she studied painting in Paris, became the youngest member of the Grand Salon at 19, then abandoned Europe to live and paint in India. She died under mysterious circumstances in Lahore in 1941, leaving behind roughly 145 paintings that are now considered national treasures — the Indian government has declared them such, making it illegal to export them.

Her work is radical even now. In the 1930s, while her contemporaries were painting British-approved landscapes and mythological scenes, Sher-Gil was documenting the lives of ordinary Indian women with a style that merged European post-impressionism with Indian folk aesthetics. She was painting poverty, solitude, and female interiority decades before anyone thought to call that "contemporary."

## Why Mira Nair, Why Now

"Every film I've made in the last several decades has been inspired by the art of Amrita Sher-Gil," Nair said when announcing the project. It's not hyperbole. Nair's entire career has been an exercise in seeing India through the eyes of someone who belongs to multiple cultures simultaneously — exactly what Sher-Gil did with a paintbrush.

The film stars Anjali Sivaraman as Sher-Gil, with Emily Watson, Jaideep Ahlawat, and Jim Sarbh rounding out the ensemble. And then there's Priyanka Chopra Jonas, whose role hasn't been specified but whose presence signals the kind of crossover ambition that could bring Sher-Gil's story to audiences who've never set foot in the National Gallery of Modern Art.

## Filming Across Three Countries

Principal photography began in January 2026 in Amritsar — near the region where Sher-Gil spent her most productive Indian years — before moving to France, where she trained at the École des Beaux-Arts, and Hungary, where she was born. The multi-country shoot mirrors the film's central tension: a woman who is simultaneously too Indian for Europe and too European for India.

This is Mira Nair's first major feature since 'A Suitable Boy' (2020), and the six-year gap suggests a project that has been meticulously incubated. The film is set for a 2027 release, with major exhibition tie-ins planned at galleries internationally.

## The Diaspora Film par Excellence

If there's a single film that embodies the Indian diaspora experience, it might be this one — and not just because of its creator. Amrita Sher-Gil's life is the original NRI story: a mixed-heritage woman navigating identity across continents, feeling the pull of India while carrying Europe in her bones. She returned to India not because she had to, but because she chose to — and found her greatest artistic voice there.

For the Indian-American, British-Indian, and Canadian-Indian communities who grew up between cultures, Sher-Gil's story isn't historical — it's personal. Mira Nair, herself a New York-based Indian filmmaker who has spent decades straddling both worlds, is perhaps the only director alive who can tell this story without turning it into either a Bollywood melodrama or a Western exoticisation.

## What to Watch For

The film's 2027 release will likely target the fall festival circuit — Cannes, Venice, or Toronto — before a theatrical run. For diaspora audiences, 'Amri' represents something rare: a prestige Indian film made by an Indian filmmaker, about an Indian artist, with global distribution ambitions that don't require compromising the story's complexity. That Priyanka Chopra's involvement virtually guarantees mainstream attention is the cherry on top.

In a year where Indian cinema is dominated by franchise sequels and box office calculations, 'Amri' is a reminder that the most powerful Indian stories are sometimes the most intimate ones.
